recipe.history:
Thyme is one of the oldest cultivated herbs in recorded human history, its roots stretching back more than four thousand years to the ancient Mediterranean basin. The Egyptians used it in embalming rituals, recognizing its powerful antimicrobial properties long before science could explain them. The Greeks burned it as incense in their temples, believing its smoke conferred courage, and the name itself likely derives from the Greek word thymos, meaning spirit or smoke. It grew wild across the rocky hillsides of Provence, Tuscany, and the Aegean coast, thriving in poor soil and full sun, its tiny grey-green leaves packed with volatile oils — thymol chief among them — that give the herb its unmistakable warm, slightly floral, faintly medicinal perfume. Romans carried it across the empire, planting it wherever they garrisoned, and by the Middle Ages it was an indispensable fixture of every European monastery garden, used to flavor everything from roasted meats to medicinal teas.

Thyme's arrival in American cooking came along several routes simultaneously. French Creole settlers planted it in Louisiana, where it became a cornerstone of the holy trinity of Cajun seasoning. English colonists brought it to New England, where it flavored roasts and stuffings. But its real ascent in American burger culture happened through the compound butter tradition — the French practice of folding softened herbs into butter and chilling it into sliceable rounds that melt luxuriously over hot meat. Steakhouses in New York and New Orleans began finishing their patties and strips with herb butters in the mid-twentieth century, and thyme — with its particular affinity for beef — became a natural choice. Roasting tomatoes with thyme concentrates their sugars while the herb perfumes the fruit, creating a topping that is simultaneously sweet, acidic, and deeply savory, a combination that transforms a simple burger into something that tastes like a Sunday afternoon in the south of France.

I remember the first time I truly understood what thyme could do. I was staying with a friend whose grandmother had a small garden in the back of her house outside of Lyon, and she sent us out one evening to cut herbs before dinner. I pulled a sprig of thyme and rubbed it between my palms and stood there for a long moment just breathing it in — that particular combination of earth and sun and something almost medicinal, something ancient. She roasted a chicken with a whole handful of it stuffed under the skin, and the kitchen filled with a smell that felt like it had been filling kitchens for centuries before either of us was born. When I came home and started experimenting with it in compound butter, pressing it into beef fat while the patty rested, I felt like I was connecting two very distant points on a very long line.

Cooking a burger to medium rare is not a preference — it is the correct answer, the destination the recipe is always trying to reach. A patty pulled from the heat at an internal temperature between 130 and 135 degrees Fahrenheit sits at the precise point where the proteins have set enough to hold their structure while the fat has rendered just enough to coat every fiber with richness. The center remains a deep rose, yielding and tender, almost custardy against the tooth. When you add a pad of thyme compound butter to that surface while the patty rests, it melts into the meat rather than sliding off a dry, overcooked surface. Well-done beef is a different food entirely — grey throughout, squeezed of its juices, the fat rendered past the point of pleasure into something grainy and dense. There is no cruelty in cooking a burger past medium rare; there is only sadness. The thyme-roasted tomatoes on this burger, warm and collapsed and fragrant, deserve a counterpart that is equally alive.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
2 tbsp fresh thyme leaves, finely chopped
1 clove garlic, minced to a paste
instructions: 1. Make the compound butter: Combine softened butter, chopped thyme, garlic paste, lemon zest, salt, and pepper in a bowl and mix thoroughly. Turn onto a sheet of plastic wrap, roll into a log about 1.5 inches in diameter, twist the ends tight, and refrigerate for at least 2 hours or up to 1 week.

2. Make the bun dough: Whisk together warm milk, yeast, and sugar in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, butter, and egg. Mix with the dough hook on medium speed for 8–10 minutes until the dough is smooth, elastic, and pulls cleanly from the sides of the bowl.
3. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise at room temperature until doubled, about 1 to 1.5 hours.

4. Divide dough into 4 equal portions (about 150g each). Shape each into a tight ball by folding the edges under and rolling on an unfloured surface. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing at least 3 inches apart. Cover loosely and let rise again until puffy and doubled, about 45 minutes.

5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush buns with egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake 16–18 minutes until deep golden brown and hollow-sounding when tapped on the bottom. Cool on a wire rack.

6. Roast the tomatoes: Increase oven to 400°F (205°C). Arrange tomato halves cut-side up on a rimmed baking sheet. Lay thyme sprigs across and around them. Drizzle with olive oil, sprinkle with sugar, salt, and pepper. Roast 35–40 minutes until collapsed, caramelized at the edges, and intensely fragrant. Remove thyme sprigs before serving.

7. Prepare the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions of about 170g each. Gently form into patties approximately 3/4 inch thick, making a slight dimple in the center of each with your thumb to prevent doming. Season both sides generously with salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Refrigerate uncovered for 15 minutes.
8. Heat a cast-iron skillet or grill pan over high heat until it begins to smoke. Cook patties 3 minutes on the first side without pressing. Flip once and cook 2–3 minutes on the second side.
9. Place a slice of fontina on each patty. Add a splash of water to the pan, cover immediately with a lid or dome, and steam for 30–45 seconds until cheese is melted.

10. Immediately transfer patties to a resting rack. Slice two rounds of thyme compound butter (about 1/4 inch thick each) and lay one on top of each hot patty. Let rest 3–4 minutes — the target internal temperature is 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. The butter will melt into the surface of the meat.
11. While patties rest, toss arugula with olive oil and lemon juice. Season lightly with salt.
12. Split and toast buns cut-side down in a dry skillet over medium heat until golden, about 1–2 minutes.

13. Assemble: Spread mayonnaise on both cut surfaces of each bun. Place patty with melted compound butter on the bottom bun. Add 2 roasted tomato halves on top of the patty. Pile dressed arugula on the tomatoes. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Set top bun in place and serve immediately.
